cap: Giant Pandas Bao Li and Qing Bao Socialize in the Snow
desc:
Snow wasn't the only thing in the air during the storm! 💕 

On Sunday, Bao Li and Qing Bao spent a lot of time interacting with each other through the “howdy” gate — a mesh screen that separates the two panda habitats— with adorable results!

Giant pandas tend to prefer their own space and usually only share habitat when they’re ready to reproduce, which is why they are housed separately at the Zoo. At just four years old, both Bao Li and Qing Bao are still a few years away from sexual maturity, which occurs around five to six years old. But keepers say the “teenage” pandas have expressed growing interest in each other lately, sharing greetings by bleating and pressing their noses against the gate. Or in Bao Li’s case, by showing off his impressive somersaulting skills.

Tune into our Panda Cam to catch all the antics by visiting https://s.si.edu/4rbOlOt

desc:

On January 25, the National Zoo's giant pandas, Bao Li and Qing Bao, took full advantage of the snow day: climbing, tumbling and playing with their toys in the snow. cap: Preparing for Pseudopregnancy with Giant Panda Qing Bao
desc: Earlier this spring, giant panda Qing Bao experienced her first estrus cycle—the very short window when female giant pandas are able to conceive a cub. She and male Bao Li didn’t breed this year, but changes in Qing Bao’s behavior and hormones indicate she’s going through pseudopregnancy—the phenomenon where a female panda behaves as if she is pregnant, even though she isn't. cap: #DCPandas: What's on the Menu for Giant Pandas?
desc:
What’s on the menu for giant pandas Bao Li and Qing Bao? About 95% of a giant panda's diet is bamboo, and they eat massive quantities to get the vitamins and nutrients they need to survive. To satisfy the bears’ voracious appetites, our giant panda team feeds them between 80 and 100 pounds of bamboo each day!
. . .
Several times a week, our Department of Nutrition staff select, harvest and deliver bamboo to the pandas’ habitat. There, it’s labeled, rinsed and kept cool with automated water misters—just like the ones that keep parsley and cilantro fresh at the grocery store. With the “meal prep” complete, it’s ready for Bao Li and Qing Bao to eat!
. . .
Keepers pay close attention to which parts of the bamboo the pandas consume. Depending on the season and the type of bamboo, Bao Li and Qing Bao might devour the leaves or the stalk of the bamboo. STORY: https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/ne....

cap: #DCPandas: Qing Bao and Bao Li Play With Puzzle Feeders
desc:
Playing with your food is always allowed at the Zoo! In the wild, giant pandas spend much of their time looking for the perfect bamboo stalks to eat. To encourage Bao Li and Qing Bao to search for their Zoo diets, our giant panda team comes up with creative ways to make mealtime fun. In addition to bamboo, treats—such as diced fruits, vegetables and panda bread—are scattered throughout the habitats. 
. . .
They’re also hidden inside puzzle feeders—toys that are built to withstand the bears’ teeth, claws and pounces. To get the food out, the pandas chase, spin and push the feeders until they reap their rewards. Bao Li and Qing Bao seem to enjoy any toy that they can swat around, jump on top of, or carry around their habitat.

cap: #DCPandas: Let the Good Times Roll, Bao Li and Qing Bao!
desc:
🐼🌀 Let the good times roll! To help giant pandas Bao Li and Qing Bao feel at home, keepers give them enrichment toys, which encourage them to be curious, play and use their natural behaviors. 
. . . 
🦪🌲Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but Qing Bao prefers pearls. Specifically, pearl balls strung together with woven yacht rope. Recently, she’s taken to carrying her favorite toy into the trees and rolling down the hill with the pearls between her paws. It’s great exercise! 
. . . 
🍎 👀 Bao Li seems to prefer toys that use both energy and brain power. Currently, his favorite toy is one where keepers hide hay and pieces of food inside. To move treats from the puzzle feeder to his belly, Bao Li spins, shakes or rolls the feeder around the yard until he has gobbled up every piece. This gives him an opportunity to use his problem-solving skills!

cap: #DCPandas: Bao Li and Qing Bao Settle In To Their New Home
desc:
🐼 A moment of pause, courtesy of giant pandas Bao Li and Qing Bao. It takes a village to make a panda feel at home. While veterinarians and nutritionists focus on the physical side of a pandas’ overall health, the goal for the animal keepers is to make sure the pandas are feeling safe and confident in their new habitat. Panda keepers record the bears’ behavior and introduce activities designed to encourage the pandas to interact with their environment. They watch for signs the animals are playful and content. 
. . . 
“We want to see the pandas eating, playing, sleeping, and exploring their exhibit,” says keeper Mariel Lally. “We want to see parts of their personalities coming out. We want to see them feel safe and confident in their new spaces. We’re doing everything we can to make this a rewarding experience not just for the pandas, but for the visitors, too.” STORY: https://s.si.edu/3AsRa9o.

cap: A Giant Farewell to Giant Pandas Tian Tian, Mei Xiang and Xiao Qi Ji
desc:
Giant pandas Tian Tian, Mei Xiang and Xiao Qi Ji began their journey to China this morning, Nov. 8, 2023. They departed the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute at 9:31 a.m. EST for Dulles International Airport in northern Virginia where they will board a dedicated and custom-decaled FedEx Panda Express Boeing 777F aircraft. The approximately 19-hour, trans-Pacific flight from Washington, D.C., to Chengdu, China, will include a brief refueling stop in Anchorage, Alaska.
. . .
First thing this morning, the panda team finalized preparations for the pandas’ departure. After receiving their breakfast, each panda entered their individual, custom travel crate, which they have been acclimating to over the past several weeks. One by one, Mei Xiang, Tian Tian and Xiao Qi Ji’s crates were moved onto a forklift that traveled carefully out of the David M. Rubenstein Family Giant Panda Habitat. They were then loaded onto FedEx trucks before departing the Zoo.
. . .
Brandie

cap: Media B-Roll: Panda Palooza at Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
desc:
Sept. 23, 2023 | This morning, Asia Trail keepers at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) in Washington, D.C., celebrated the kick-off of Panda Palooza at the David M. Rubenstein Family Giant Panda Habitat. At 9 a.m., animal care staff presented all three giant pandas with a special panda-friendly fruitsicle cake made by the Zoo’s Department of Nutrition Science. desc: Although we still see Xiao Qi Ji nurse for comfort from time to time, the majority of his diet is made up of bamboo, fruit and high fiber biscuits. He receives his own diet twice a day; we feed him separately from Mei Xiang to ensure she does not eat his portions. Lately, he has become much more efficient at eating—not to mention protective of his treats. If Mei Xiang dares to come near “his” food, he can be seen and heard giving her a piece of his mind! When Xiao Qi Ji chooses to follow Mei Xiang around, he usually tries to sneak a bite of whatever she’s eating. He is growing nicely. At his last weigh-in, he tipped the scales at 72 pounds. This time last year—when he was just 9 weeks old—he weighed 7.5 pounds!

cap: Giant Panda Cub: Name Reveal
desc: The Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute’s 3-month-old giant panda cub received his name today. After five days of voting and just under 135,000 votes, the winning name is Xiao Qi Ji (SHIAU-chi-ji), which translates as “little miracle” in English. It was one of four Mandarin Chinese names that were offered for a public online vote from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 on the Zoo’s website. Giant pandas are an international symbol of endangered wildlife and hope, and Xiao Qi Ji’s birth offered the world a much-needed moment of joy amidst the COVID-19 pandemic. His name reflects the extraordinary circumstances under which he was born and celebrates the collaboration between colleagues who strive to conserve this species. cap: It's a Boy! Smithsonian’s National Zoo’s Giant Panda Cub Is Male
desc:
The Smithsonian’s National Zoo’s 6-week-old giant panda cub is a male, Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute (SCBI) scientists confirmed. During the cub’s first veterinary exam Sept. 19, Zoo veterinarians obtained a swab from his cheek for DNA analysis. Outwardly, male and female cubs appear similar at birth, so a genetic test was the most accurate way to determine the cub’s sex. Veterinarians brought the swab to SCBI’s Center for Conservation Genomics, where scientists sequenced a short fragment of the zinc finger protein gene. The X and Y chromosomes both have this gene, with slightly different DNA sequences. Scientists determined that the swab sample taken by the Zoo’s veterinarians has both sequences present—confirming that the cub is male. A painting created by male giant panda Tian Tian (tee-YEN tee-YEN), the cub’s father, was used to reveal the sex of the cub to giant panda keepers and fans online.

cap: Mei Xiang Playing in a Bubble Bath Tub
desc:
On March 15, Mei Xiang started exhibiting behavioral signs that breeding season is approaching! A urinary hormone analysis confirmed that her change in behavior was due to her rising estrogen levels, signaling that the panda breeding season will be here soon.

Mei Xiang’s behavioral changes have not been especially subtle, she has broken from her energy-efficient routine of eating and sleeping and is instead much more active. She is very eager to play and splash in the pools in her yard and enclosure, and the bubble bath tubs she receives as extra enrichment. She also has been scent-marking around her habitat. Scent-marks are one of the ways giant pandas communicate if they are ready to breed. Adults do not spend time together outside of the breeding season. cap: Bei Bei Celebrates His Third Birthday at the Smithsonian's National Zoo
desc: Giant panda Bei Bei (BAY BAY) celebrated his third birthday at the Smithsonian's National Zoo. He was born at the Zoo Aug. 22, 2015, to mother Mei Xiang (may-SHONG) and father Tian Tian (t-YEN t-YEN) as the result of artificial insemination. His name means “precious” or “treasure.” Bei Bei currently weighs 214 pounds. Each giant panda has distinctive markings; Bei Bei’s eye patches are heart-shaped, and two black dots sit on the bridge of his nose.

cap: Making Bei Bei's New Hammock
desc: The exhibits team built the hammocks from sturdy fire hose and installed them. There has been a hammock in Bei Bei’s enclosure for several years, but it was starting to show some wear-and-tear as it’s been a favorite resting spot for him and Bao Bao when she lived there. Bei Bei is 215 pounds now and still growing, so our exhibits team made the hammock large enough for an adult male. That also means that if Mei Xiang or Tian Tian spend time in that enclosure, the hammock will be big enough to accommodate them.

cap: Mei Xiang Participates in an Ultrasound
desc: The only definitive way to determine if Mei Xiang is pregnant before she gives birth is to detect a fetus on an ultrasound. Veterinarians have are conducting ultrasounds twice a week to track changes in Mei Xiang’s reproductive tract, but it is still too early to see a developing fetus on an ultrasound. It is important that Mei Xiang is comfortable with the procedure and is trained to participate in it because she is more reactive to change and unfamiliar things at the end of a pregnancy or pseudopregnancy. If she is trained to participate in and is comfortable with having an ultrasound, it increases the chances she will participate in the final stages of a pregnancy or pseudopregnancy. However, she always has the choice to participate. If she chooses not to participate, she can leave the training chute at any time and veterinarians will not perform an ultrasound.

cap: Giant Panda Plays with Ice (Treat) Hockey Puck

cap: Giant Panda Mei Xiang Receives an Ultrasound
desc: Aug. 11, 2017—Veterinarians at the Smithsonian's National Zoo performing an ultrasound on giant panda Mei Xiang Aug. 3. It is too soon to determine if she is pregnant, but veterinarians are tracking changes in her uterus. Keepers work with Mei Xiang to voluntarily participate in ultrasounds. She enters a training chute where she lies down and presents her belly to veterinarians. Keepers offer Mei Xiang some of her favorite treats, such as honey water and pears, for participating in the ultrasound. She also likes to scent-anoint her self with the ultrasound gel after the procedure is complete. The only way to definitively determine if a female giant panda is pregnant is to detect a fetus on an ultrasound. Her hormones and behavior will mimic a pregnancy even if she is not pregnant.

cap: Giant Panda Cub Veterinary Exam
desc: At a veterinary exam Sept. 17, 2015 our giant panda cub measured 31 centimeters from his head to the tip of his tail. From his head to the base of his tail he measured 27 centimeters. His right front leg was 10 centimeters long and his right hind leg was 9 centimeters long. Veterinarians reported that he has an excellent range of motion and is able to push up onto his front legs. Keepers have seen him scooting around the den using his front legs, but he is not walking yet. #PandaStory

cap: GoPro Footage of Giant Panda Cub Exam
desc:
Mei Xiang left her den Saturday afternoon to eat and drink. She ate more bamboo than during her previous excursions away from the den, which is normal. Keepers expect Mei Xiang to gradually spend more time away from the den eating and drinking as the cub grows. While Mei Xiang was eating, veterinarians and keepers took the opportunity to give the cub another quick checkup. He weighed 409.6 grams, which was 119 grams more than he weighed on Sept. 2. His 297 percent weight increase is normal for a cub his age. Cubs at this stage usually gain between 40 and 55 grams per day. Veterinarians also listened to his heart and lungs, which all sounded normal. His eyes are still closed, which is normal. Cubs’ eyes generally open when they are 6 to 8 weeks old. He also had a full belly at the time of the exam and appeared to be healthy. ‪#‎PandaStory‬

Sept. 5, 2015

cap: Giant Panda Cub Health Check
desc:
Mei Xiang left her den for a few minutes Wednesday afternoon giving our veterinarians an opportunity to do a quick cub health check to ensure that he is growing and healthy. They listened to his heart and lungs, palpated his abdomen and checked that he was able to move his forelimbs and hindlimbs. He is moving well and had a full belly. He now weighs in at 287.5 grams (about 10 ounces)! His eyes are still closed and his black markings are becoming more pronounced. #PandaStory

She put the cub down when she left and he was very quiet the entire time she was gone. Over the next few weeks she will get more comfortable leaving him for increasingly longer periods of time to eat and drink. While Mei was away, our behavior watchers got a fantastic view of the cub!

cap: Giant Panda Cub is a Boy!
desc: Aug. 28, 2015. Scientists at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute’s Center for Conservation and Evolutionary Genetics confirmed that the giant panda cub born to Mei Xiang Aug. 22 at the National Zoo is male. A paternity analysis showed that Tian Tian is the cub’s father.

cap: Mei Xiang and Cub
desc:
Overnight, it was evident to panda keepers and veterinarians that our healthy panda cub was active and nursing appropriately throughout the night. Mother Mei Xiang is showing proper maternal care which includes short sleep cycles and adjusting the tiny cub in her arms for better positioning and grooming. The staff heard strong vocalizations from the cub and observed it a couple times during the night. The cub is growing more hair, its tail looks plump and the cub overall looks great. The Zoo will continue to provide daily updates on Mei Xiang and the cub through its @SmithsonianZoo Instagram account using #PandaStory and through the Giant Panda e-newsletter.

cap: Giant Panda Mei Xiang Ultrasound
desc:
Veterinarians Viewed Surprising Giant Panda Ultrasound at Smithsonian’s National Zoo

For the first time at the National Zoo, veterinarians detected something new during an ultrasound procedure this morning on giant panda Mei Xiang. They believe it is a developing giant panda fetus. Based on the size of the fetus, which is about four centimeters, veterinarians estimate that Mei Xiang could give birth early next week, or possibly in early September. In past years, veterinarians have only detected changes to Mei Xiang’s uterus, which occurs for both a pregnancy and pseudopregnancy. Historically, and since Aug. 7 of this year, Mei Xiang declined participating in ultrasounds at this stage, so it was a surprise when she responded to the panda keepers’ calls this morning.

There is a substantial possibility that Mei Xiang could resorb or miscarry a fetus. Scientists do not fully understand why some mammals resorb fetuses.

cap: Training With Bao Bao
desc: October 2014—Training is an important part of caring for giant pandas. Our adult giant pandas, Mei Xiang and Tian Tian, choose to participate in veterinary exams, like ultrasounds and blood draws. They also present their paws when asked and open their mouths, so keepers can visually check them. As a reward for choosing to interact with the keepers, the pandas get a treat, usually honey water, biscuits, apple or pear. Bao Bao is still a beginner when it comes to training, but she's making great progress. By the time she is an adult bear, she will be able to do as many behaviors as her parents. cap: National Zoo Giant Panda Shows Cub to Panda Cam Viewers
desc:
At approximately 10:09 p.m. Sept. 20, Panda Cam viewers got what may be the best view yet of the Smithsonian's National Zoo's five-day-old panda cub. Balanced atop mother Mei Xiang's arm, the cub squirms and vocalizes while being groomed. 

Zoo staff and volunteers are diligently monitoring both bears over the Panda Cam along with tens of thousands of panda enthusiasts. Viewers can help the Zoo capture video by taking a screen grab and sharing it on Flickr.

To follow the panda cub's progress, read the updates from the Zoo's panda keepers and check for news on the Zoo's Twitter feed and Facebook page. We will continue to send media alerts about cub developments.

cap: Panda Cub at the Smithsonian's National Zoo
desc:
The Smithsonian's National Zoo's female giant panda Mei Xiang gave Panda Cam viewers another sneak peek of her cub, born Sunday Sept. 16. At about 7:54 a.m. Sept. 20, Mei Xiang gently picked the squealing cub up in her mouth before placing it on the ground to groom it. Keepers continue to be encouraged by the cub's activity and vocalizations—two signs that it is healthy. Mei Xiang is able to sleep for brief periods but promptly cradles, grooms and nurses her cub when it vocalizes. Zoo staff and volunteers are diligently monitoring both bears over the Panda Cam, minimizing disturbances around their den. The behavior studies are an integral part of the Zoo's research effort to better understand the species' reproductive physiology. We will continue to send media alerts about cub developments. 

To follow the panda cub's progress, read the updates from the Zoo's panda keepers and check for news on the Zoo's Twitter feed and Facebook page.

cap: Glimpse of the Smithsonian's National Zoo's Panda Cub
desc: Smithsonian's National Zoo staff and Panda Cam watchers have gotten several quick glimpses of female giant panda Mei Xiang's cub.  In this video, Sept. 17. at about 8:35 p.m. EST, Mei Xiang cradles the newborn and gently picks it up in her mouth as she shifts position.  This is normal behavior and another sign that Mei Xiang is being an excellent mother to her new cub.  By using her mouth, Mei Xiang can very gently and dexterously position her cub on her body so that she is able to nurse and groom it.  The cub actively squirms and vocalizes loudly in response—two good signs that the cub is healthy! Keepers report that Mei Xiang is exhibiting excellent maternal behaviors. She is prompt to cradle and groom the cub, and there is evidence that it is successfully nursing. The Zoo will continue to diligently monitor both bears over the Panda Cam and minimize disturbances around their den.

cap: Footage of giant panda birth at the Smithsonian's National Zoo
desc:
As panda cam watchers may have noticed: from Mei's behavior and the sounds we're hearing, we have a giant panda cub!

As far as we can tell, the cub was born at about 10:46 p.m. on September 16. According to chief veterinarian Suzan Murray:

"Mei Xiang is behaving exactly the same way she did when Tai Shan was born. She is cradling her cub closely , and she looks so tired, but every time she tries to lay down, the cub squawks and she sits right up and cradles the cub more closely. She is the poster child for a perfect panda mom."

We believe there is only one cub. If the cub is to have a twin, we should know by sunrise.

For now, the only way animal care staff will monitor the cub is using the web cams. Our goal is for Mei Xiang to raise this cub naturally. With Tai Shan, it wasn't until he was about two weeks old that Mei walked away from him briefly and our veterinary team was able to give him a brief well-cub exam.

Keep your eyes on the panda cam and on our website and social media

cap: Smithsonian's National Zoo Receives $4.5 Million for Giant Panda Program
desc: David M. Rubenstein donated $4.5 million to the Smithsonian's National Zoo to fund the giant panda program for the next five years. The gift will be used to fund conservation efforts in China, reproductive science, professional training programs, giant panda care at the Zoo, upgrades to the Zoo habitats and public education. In appreciation, the giant panda complex—home to giant pandas Tian Tian (male) and Mei Xiang (female)—will be named the David M. Rubenstein Family Giant Panda Habitat. In addition, young conservation biologists in the U.S. and in China who are awarded National Zoo fellowships for their work to save this endangered species will be named "David M. Rubenstein Fellows."

cap: #PandaStory: Xiao Qi Ji Weaning
desc:
Xiao Qi Ji is on a roll! The winter winds may blow chilly and cold, but they also bring out the sillies in our giant panda cub. On Jan. 19, the frisky 2.5-year-old tumbled around his outdoor habitat and showed off his unique somersault style.  

Solo play sessions such as this help our giant panda team evaluate how Xiao Qi Ji is adjusting to spending time apart from his mother, Mei Xiang. Keepers give them access to different habitats in the morning, then reunite them in the afternoon and evening. They have noticed that Mei Xiang appears to have less patience with Xiao Qi Ji’s rambunctious antics and will vocalize or chase him when she is not in the mood to play. As we have shared in previous #PandaStory updates, his growing confidence and comfortability with spending time alone are encouraging signs that he’s growing up and getting ready to be on his own.
